title_zh: 可以退出，为什么不能一笔勾销？
title_en: Leaving Does Not Erase the Account
deck_zh: 一项允许个人申诉的条款，被正在受问的国家退出了。它能走；失去通道的人却没有因此得到回答。怎样既不锁住成员，也不把留下的问题说没了？
deck_en: A country withdraws from the very petition procedure questioning it. It can leave. The people losing that route have not thereby received an answer. Both facts must stay in view.
body_zh: 那两个人已经服刑几年了。一个判十二年，一个判九年，审理不公开，辩护人由法院指定。他们曾是麦原临时自治委员会的委员；外军撤走以后，大多数委员随之离开，留下的两人被共和国以协敌起诉。
共和国加入三界协作体系，后来接受了允许个人申诉的第十四条。两人于是经家属和律师向委员会申诉。原判发生在条款生效以前，但上诉被驳回、关押继续，都在生效以后；委员会依约受理了这段持续的影响。
委员会要求审理记录，申请探视。共和国先答了一句，审判依本国法律进行；随后，正在答问的外务部经主席批准，声明退出第十四条，不再就这件申诉作答。一个原本用来问的门，就这样被正在门后的人关上了。
## 门能关上，关门这件事仍须回答
能不能拦住它？若拦不住，个人申诉是否就只是愿意听时才听的摆设？这两个问题不能靠“退出是权利”轻轻带过。那句话只说出了共和国的一面，尚未说到两个人和后来七件新申诉失去的是什么。
先看共和国自己的决定。接受条款时，人民议会投过票；退出时却没有。六十一位议员联名要求表决，主席团没有排入议程。退出可以是本国的决定，不等于正在被问的那个位置就该独自作完决定。谁能审查，受影响的人怎样提出异议，首先在本国内部就有一整层问题。
体系也可以审查，记下时间与理由，问退出为何发生在受问期间。能审查，不等于拥有最后的批准权。若共同机关可以说“我不同意，所以你不能离开”，并强行维持成员身份，它便不再只是平级者之间的协作。
这不等于凡是通知就必须立即散场。事先认下的通知期、过渡安排、尚未结清的事项，都要认真对待。但是退出的终点不能被被退出的一方不断延长，直到对方满足一切要求。可以留下未结的账，不能把账做成永远打不开的锁。
共和国的声明满十二个月生效。生效以前已经提出的申诉照常审结，以后提出的则不受理。这个规则是故事选择的一种写法，不是散文替所有现实机构推荐的最佳条款。它最不方便的后果，也必须照实写出来。
第十九年春，七件新申诉被退回。说“外部追问还在”，不能把这七次退回说成没有发生。别国可以继续提问，记录可以留下，却并不等于原来那条能由个人发动的程序还在。一个真实丢失的入口，不应被一句更大的原则代替。
退出还会有别的锁法。若体系越过成员自己的法，拿走成员自己的储备，或用能够直接落地的命令阻止离开，那么不论它仍叫什么，实际上已经取得了另一种权力。讨论这种上级怎样受到约束是必要的，只是不能继续用“我们只是协作”躲开。
在这里，离开不是一张不必受问的证明。关门的决定可以一直被问，问题却不能变成锁住门的强制。把这两件事分开，很难让任何一方完全满意，但至少不会把批评误写成拘禁，也不会把退出误写成清白。
## 人离开了桌子，旧事还在
退出究竟终止什么？首先是往后以成员身份新增、行使的权利与义务，不是把过去所有事情改写为从未发生。最直观的分法，是沿着时间往前看：成员期间做过的，已经开始处理的，退出以后才来请求处理的，三件分别回答。
成员期间的行动照记。共和国两人继续关押，石峡邦在退出通知期里不答营地申诉，都发生在相应承诺有效的时候。不能因为日后不再参与，便把当时承担过什么从纸上擦掉。记在国家名下，也要记到作决定的位置。
已经开始的程序，则依约走完。委员会第十八年冬提出意见，请共和国公开复审，准许探视；共和国仍未答。程序可以审结，回答却未必到来。若写成“申诉得到处理”，读者很容易误以为两个人的处境因此已经改善。
他们到第二十年仍在关押，一人转入监所医院。这不是应该放在脚注里的小遗憾，而是这套安排没有强制落实能力的具体样子。问到了，记下了，程序走完了，人还没有出来。几件事可以同时是真的。
退出以后，对以前的事情还能不能新开程序，要对已经认下的约，不由我们凭愿望补。这个例子规定生效后新提出的一律不受理，所以七件退回就是失去了一条路。约若另有存续安排，则按那项安排处理，不能把一种规则说成所有规则的必然。
旧账也不是无穷的道德绳索。共同资源、程序义务、过渡经费，要明确送到怎样的安排里去，不能只说你永远还欠着。石峡邦退出后，依原约仍收到下一年上半年的营地分担经费，转送也继续到当年夏天。已经约定存续的部分，没有因退出立即停掉。
同时，从退出生效起，石峡邦不能再以成员身份请求启动新的共同程序。不能只保留往后的好处，却把过去认下的承担全都叫作结束了。各项权利义务在哪个时点止、哪些继续，得一项项说清，不靠一个“退出”包办。
还记得那位在石峡邦申请庇护的指挥官设例吗？石峡邦离开宪约，条约层面的承诺向后停止；不把门口的人送回杀害、酷刑或不经审判拘押的地方，却不是成员资格送给它的责任。退出一份约，并不能顺便退出自己正在对具体的人做的事。
所以，走是真的，账也是真的。若说还有责任就不算走，离开只剩名义；若说已经走了就什么都不用答，那些曾受其行动影响的人又会在程序变动中被一起删掉。难处不是选一句更响亮的话，而是把两者都落到具体的时间和事项上。
## 回来，是重新订一份约
石峡邦退出以后，灯岛驻军撤了，管理所关闭，部分居民陆续回去。代价写在它与高原联邦的新协定里：提前通知、免于登记的舰队通行，二十五年的补给码头租用，以及不参加任何针对高原联邦的多边经济措施。
后来石峡邦换了政府，又申请回到体系。伙伴提出三件事：两件旧申诉怎样答，补给码头怎样处理，那条预先拒绝一切多边措施的承诺又怎么办。共和国代表说，走是权利，回来也是。听起来对称，事情却并不对称。
走，是改变自己参与的安排；回来，是重新建立彼此的约束。新约要别人同意，不能单方宣布已经重新成为伙伴。各方可以提出以行动和责任为根据的条件，却不能拿接纳逼申请者改变原本没有越线的自主选择。
石峡邦说，愿意回答两件申诉，也愿意对今后每项措施分别说明是否参加；但是与高原联邦的约，不能自己单方面改掉。到第二十年冬，申请仍未决。我们不用替它安排一个终于重聚的结尾，才能看见回来为什么比敲一次门复杂。
两件事有底线：重新加入不洗掉离开期间的账；正在接管、殖民别国的行为，也不能带着它重新加入。至于什么先答、什么后谈，具体条件怎样定，交给各方公开说明与判断。不对一个国名永久封门，才让此刻的改变仍有意义。
那体系能不能主动开除一个成员？在这里可以讨论，但它也必须回答。开除针对国家的成员资格，不是把其中的人宣布为不值得保护的人；开除不能销账，也不能把一个成员早已开始的进入改写成与体系毫无关系的外部事件。
开除还可能伤到本想保护的人。既有申诉依约继续，体系自己日后的行动仍须受问；可是那一国此后行动的受影响者，可能再也进不了针对该国的成员申诉程序。失去这条路是实际代价，也是为什么不能把开除只写成一次利落的清理。
甚至体系本身解散，也要问记录放在哪里，未结的程序交给谁，共同资源怎样安排。尽量安排不等于一定安排得完；没接住的应当明说，不能因为最后一次会议已经散场，就宣布从此没有人再有问题。
两个人仍在监所，七件申诉被退回，石峡邦的申请还在等。这篇没有一个把所有线头都收齐的结局。它想留下的是更具体的读法：看到“退出”“恢复关系”“开除”这样的词，再问一句，究竟哪项关系结束了，哪件事还没有得到回答，而那个没有得到回答的人，现在还能去哪扇门。
body_en: Two men are serving sentences of twelve and nine years. Their trial was closed, their lawyers appointed by the court. They had remained behind when most members of a temporary council left with a withdrawing foreign army. DRP prosecuted them for collaboration. Years later, detention is still the most immediate fact of their lives.

DRP joins Three-Borders and accepts Article Fourteen, the individual-petition procedure. Relatives and a lawyer bring the case. The original convictions predate the provision’s operation for DRP, but the rejected appeal and continuing imprisonment follow it. The committee accepts the continuing effects under the agreed rule. It requests trial records and a prison visit.

DRP first answers that the trial followed national law. Then the foreign ministry, with presidential approval, withdraws from Article Fourteen and says it will no longer answer this petition. The procedure being questioned has an exit, and the very office receiving the questions has used it. What becomes of the people waiting outside?
## A door can close without closing the question

Can the system stop the withdrawal? If it cannot, is petitioning only a courtesy extended while governments feel agreeable? ‘Withdrawal is a right’ does not settle those questions. It describes one side of the decision, not what the two men—and seven later petitioners—are losing.

Begin inside DRP. Its assembly voted to accept Article Fourteen, but did not vote to leave. Sixty-one legislators demand a vote; the presidium does not schedule one. Calling withdrawal a national decision cannot establish that the office currently being questioned should make it alone. Domestic scrutiny is itself at issue.

The system can scrutinize the decision too, record its timing and reasons, and ask why departure occurs during an inquiry. Scrutiny is not a final power of approval. An institution able to say ‘you may not leave because we refuse permission’ and enforce continued membership has acquired something beyond coordination among equals.

This does not require every departure to take effect immediately. Agreed notice periods, transition arrangements and unsettled obligations matter. But the party being left cannot keep extending the endpoint until every demand is met. An unsettled account may survive departure; it cannot become a lock with no usable release.

DRP’s declaration takes effect after twelve months. Petitions already filed continue; new ones after that date are inadmissible. This is one rule chosen for the invented case, not a recommendation that every actual institution adopt it. Its least attractive consequences belong in the account as much as its formal clarity.

In spring of Year Nineteen, seven new petitions are returned. Saying ‘external questioning continues’ must not make those seven refusals disappear. Other countries can ask and records can remain, but neither reproduces the procedure individuals could previously initiate. A lost entrance cannot be replaced by a larger-sounding principle.

There are other ways to lock members in. If the system seizes a member’s own reserves or imposes a decision over its domestic law to prevent departure, its name does not settle what power it has acquired. That superior power would need its own safeguards. ‘We merely cooperate’ would no longer answer the question.

Leaving is therefore not proof that there is nothing to answer. The decision to close a route remains open to challenge, without that challenge becoming a coercive means of preventing departure. Neither side may find this entirely satisfying. It at least keeps criticism distinct from confinement, and exit distinct from innocence.
## Leaving the table does not erase what happened

What does withdrawal terminate? Primarily, the future relationship through which member rights and obligations are newly acquired or exercised—not the fact of everything previously done. Three time-based questions help: what happened during membership, what proceedings already began, and what someone seeks to initiate only after departure.

Conduct during membership stays on the record. The continuing imprisonment in DRP and Stonegorge’s unanswered camp petitions during its notice period occurred while the relevant commitments applied. Later departure cannot remove what was undertaken then. The entries need both the state’s address and the offices responsible for particular decisions.

Proceedings already initiated continue according to the agreement. In winter of Year Eighteen the committee asks DRP to reopen the trial publicly and allow a visit. DRP does not answer. The procedure can reach its conclusion while the requested response never comes. Saying ‘the petition was dealt with’ would risk suggesting that the prisoners’ situation improved.

By Year Twenty both remain imprisoned; one has moved to the prison hospital. This is not a minor disappointment for a footnote. It is the absence of enforcement made concrete. Questions reached their address, an opinion was issued, and the men did not come out. All of these facts can be true together.

Whether a new proceeding can begin after withdrawal about earlier conduct depends on the accepted agreement. Here the rule excludes all newly filed petitions after the effective date. The seven returned petitions therefore represent an actual loss. An agreement with different surviving jurisdiction would produce a different answer; wishes cannot fill the gap in this one.

Nor is an old account an endless moral tether. Shared resources, procedural obligations and transitional funding need identifiable arrangements, not an indefinite announcement that something remains owed. After Stonegorge leaves, agreed camp funding continues for the next half-year, and transfers continue until summer. Departure does not immediately cancel what the original agreement expressly preserves.

At the same time, Stonegorge can no longer initiate new common proceedings in the capacity of a member. It cannot retain every future benefit while calling all its accepted responsibilities finished. Which rights stop, which obligations survive and on what date require separate answers. The word withdrawal cannot do all that work alone.

Recall the hypothetical commander seeking asylum in Stonegorge. Withdrawal ends the compact’s future treaty-based constraint, but the responsibility not to return an arrival to killing, torture or detention without trial did not originate in membership. Leaving an agreement cannot also mean leaving behind responsibility for what one is presently doing to a particular person.

Departure is real; the account is real too. If any surviving responsibility means one has not truly left, exit becomes nominal. If leaving means no previous question remains, people affected by earlier decisions disappear with a procedural change. The task is to connect both facts to particular dates and matters, rather than choose the louder slogan.
## Returning makes a new agreement

After Stonegorge’s withdrawal, troops leave Lamp Island, the navigation office closes and some displaced residents return. Its agreement with the Federation also provides inspection-free passage after notification, a twenty-five-year supply-wharf lease and a promise not to participate in any multilateral economic measures against the Federation. Relief arrives with consequential terms.

A new Stonegorge government later applies to return. Partners raise the two unanswered petitions, the wharf and the blanket promise about future measures. DRP’s representative argues that if leaving is a right, returning is one too. The sentence sounds symmetrical. The two decisions are not.

Leaving changes one’s own participation. Returning establishes obligations with others again. A new agreement needs their consent; one cannot announce renewed partnership unilaterally. Partners may propose conditions grounded in conduct and responsibility, but readmission cannot become a means of forcing changes to otherwise autonomous choices that infringe no one’s standing.

Stonegorge offers to answer the petitions and explain participation in each future measure separately. It cannot, it says, unilaterally alter its agreement with the Federation. The application is unresolved at the end of Year Twenty. We do not need a reunion to see why returning is more complicated than knocking once.

Two boundaries remain: readmission does not launder conduct during absence, and an ongoing colonial takeover cannot be carried back into membership. Conditions above those boundaries—what must precede what, and how outstanding matters are handled—require public explanation and judgment. No country’s name receives a permanent ban irrespective of present conduct.

Can a system expel a member instead? Here it can, under demanding conditions, but expulsion must also answer for itself. It ends a state’s membership, not the standing of its people. It does not erase accounts or transform an incursion begun by a member into something that was always wholly external to the system.

Expulsion may also cost people a route meant to protect them. Existing petitions continue as agreed; the system remains answerable for its own subsequent conduct. But people affected by the expelled state’s later acts may lose the member-petition route against that state. This is a real cost, not an inconvenience to omit from a satisfying story of removal.

Even dissolution of the entire system raises questions: who holds the records, where do pending proceedings go, and what happens to common resources? Making the best possible arrangements does not guarantee complete arrangements. The final meeting’s adjournment cannot establish that nobody has an unanswered question left.

Two men remain in prison, seven petitions have been returned and Stonegorge’s application waits. There is no ending that gathers every thread. Instead, when we encounter withdrawal, restored relations or expulsion, we can ask something precise: which relationship has ended, which matter remains unanswered, and which door can the person still waiting now approach?
